title: Water in the Desert and a Sacrifice on the Wall
summary: Jehoram son of Ahab becomes king of Israel and, with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, marches against Mesha of Moab, who has stopped paying tribute. When the armies run out of water, Elisha promises water without rain and victory over Moab, and both come to pass. But when Mesha, trapped in his last city, offers his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the wall, great fury falls on Israel and the armies withdraw.
story: The rebellion of Moab, mentioned in passing in 1:1, now comes to a head. The chapter introduces Jehoram (also spelled Joram), Ahab's second son to reign, who is less devoted to Baal than his parents but holds to Jeroboam's calves. It is also the first story in which Elisha acts as a public prophet to kings, and it shows him with the same blunt independence as Elijah. The alliance of Israel and Judah that ended in disaster at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kings 22) is repeated almost word for word, with Jehoshaphat again asking for a prophet of the LORD. The strange ending, with victory snatched away, prepares for chapters in which Israel's kings keep winning battles by the prophet's word and keep failing to change.
historical:
Jehoram reigned in Samaria about 852 to 841 BC. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a plateau of pasture and farmland suited to sheep, and its tribute of lambs and wool (verse 4) reflects its economy. Moab had been subject to Israel since the days of Omri. The Mesha Stele, a black basalt inscription found at Dhiban (biblical Dibon) in 1868 and now in the Louvre, is Mesha's own record. In it Mesha says that Omri had oppressed Moab for many days because the Moabite god Chemosh was angry with his land, that Omri's son continued the oppression, and that Mesha threw off Israel's control, took Israelite towns north of the Arnon, and built up his cities. The stele does not describe the campaign of 2 Kings 3, and the two accounts are hard to fit together in detail, but they agree on the main fact: Moab under Mesha broke free of Israel in this period.

The allies went around the southern end of the Dead Sea through Edom, perhaps to avoid Moab's fortified northern border. Edom at this time was a vassal of Judah; 1 Kings 22:47 notes that a deputy ruled it, and the king of Edom here is likely such a dependent ruler. Kir-haraseth, Moab's stronghold, is usually identified with modern Kerak in Jordan, a naturally fortified hilltop. The sudden water in verse 20 fits a known feature of the region: rain in the Edomite highlands can send flash floods down dry valleys far from where any rain falls.
cultural:
Kings routinely consulted prophets before battle, and Jehoshaphat's request for a prophet of the LORD repeats his instinct from 1 Kings 22. Elisha is identified as the one who used to pour water on the hands of Elijah, a phrase describing a personal servant or disciple. Music was associated with prophecy in Israel (compare 1 Samuel 10:5), and Elisha asks for a musician before the hand of the LORD comes on him. The ordered destruction of trees, springs, and fields in verse 19 was a way of crippling an enemy's economy for years; it stands in tension with Deuteronomy 20:19-20, which forbids cutting down fruit trees in a siege, and interpreters differ on whether Elisha's word is a prediction of what will happen or a command.

Child sacrifice was practiced in parts of the ancient Mediterranean world, particularly in times of crisis, and Israel's law forbade it absolutely (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). Mesha offered his firstborn heir as a burnt offering, presumably to Chemosh, on the city wall in sight of the besiegers, an act of desperate appeal to his god. The Mesha Stele shows how Moab understood its history in terms of Chemosh's anger and favor, much as Israel understood its history in terms of the LORD's.
literary: The chapter opens with a regnal formula for Jehoram and then tells a story with a familiar shape: kings in trouble, a prophet sought, a word given, and the word fulfilled. The echoes of 1 Kings 22 are deliberate, including Jehoshaphat's pledge, “I am like you, my people are your people, and my horses are your horses” (verse 7). Elisha's word in verses 16-19 has two parts, water and victory, and the narrative carries out both. The water theme ties the chapter together: the armies have no water, water comes without wind or rain, and the same water, red in the morning sun, deceives the Moabites into thinking it is blood. The ending is abrupt and unresolved. After verse after verse of fulfillment, the last verse reverses the outcome, and the narrator declines to explain it.

outline.t: Mesha rebels and three kings march against Moab
No water, and a prophet sought
Elisha's word: ditches, water, and victory

doctrines.note: God provides water in a dry valley by means the soldiers never see, with neither wind nor rain. He works through natural processes and at his own time, “at the time of the morning sacrifice” (verse 20).
Elisha's word comes when the hand of the LORD is on him, and it holds true in every detail. Even a king he refuses to honor benefits from the word for Jehoshaphat's sake.

Mesha's sacrifice of his son shows where the worship of false gods can lead: to the destruction of what a person loves most in hope of buying a god's help. Israel's law named this practice an abomination.

words.note: Qetseph, wrath or fury. The great fury against Israel in verse 27 is the chapter's puzzle. Elsewhere in the Old Testament qetseph usually refers to the LORD's wrath, which is one reason some interpreters think God's anger fell on Israel. The word itself does not say whose fury it was.

Olah, burnt offering, a sacrifice wholly consumed on the altar. It is the word used for Israel's daily offerings to the LORD, and its use here for the Moabite king's son is shocking by design. It also recalls the testing of Abraham, where Isaac was to be offered as an olah and God provided a ram instead (Genesis 22:2, 13).

Nagan, to play a stringed instrument. Elisha asks for a musician, and while he plays the hand of the LORD comes on the prophet. The same verb is used of David playing the lyre before Saul (1 Samuel 16:23). The scene shows music as a setting for receiving God's word, without suggesting it produces it.

christ: The chapter's darkest moment points by contrast toward the gospel. A king, desperate to save his city, offers his firstborn son to his god, and the result is horror. The Old Testament consistently condemns such offerings, and the prophet Micah asks whether one should give one's firstborn for one's own sin, only to answer that God requires justice, kindness, and humble walking (Micah 6:7-8). The New Testament proclaims something entirely different: not a man giving his son to win over a god, but God himself giving his own Son out of love (John 3:16; Romans 8:32), a gift received rather than a price paid to an angry deity. The link is a contrast, not a type. The chapter also shows water given in the desert as a free gift of God, a theme the New Testament develops when Jesus offers living water (John 4:10).

hard.q: Why did Israel withdraw after Mesha sacrificed his son, and whose fury fell on them?
hard.a: The text says only that there was great fury against Israel, and interpreters have long disagreed about what that means. One view is that the LORD's anger fell on Israel, because qetseph most often refers to divine wrath; on this reading Israel may have provoked it by the excess of the campaign, the destruction of trees and fields, or by something that made Israel complicit in the horror, though the text does not say what. A second view is that the fury was human: Israel's own horror and revulsion at the sight, or Moab's rage and renewed resistance, or Edom's anger (the Moabite king had tried to break through to the king of Edom), which broke the alliance. A third view, held by some critical scholars, is that the story preserves the Moabite belief that Chemosh's anger drove Israel back, without the narrator endorsing Chemosh's reality. What the chapter does not do is suggest that the sacrifice was effective in the sense Mesha hoped; the rest of Scripture condemns it. The narrator leaves the ending unexplained, and the honest reading acknowledges the uncertainty.

questions: Elisha said the water would come without wind or rain. When has help come to you by a route you did not see coming?
The prophet helped Jehoram only for Jehoshaphat's sake. What does it mean that one faithful person can bring blessing to others around them?
Mesha gave up his son in hope of saving his city. What do people sacrifice today to the things they hope will save them?
